text: If CAT is written as DBU, how is DOG written in the same code?
explanation: Each letter moves one place forward: C-D, A-B, T-U. Applying that to DOG gives E, P, H, so EPH. Moving backwards instead gives CNF.

text: If PEN is written as 16-5-14, how is BAG written in the same code?
explanation: Each letter is replaced by its position in the alphabet: P is 16, E is 5, N is 14. So B is 2, A is 1, G is 7, giving 2-1-7.

text: If LAMP is written as MBNQ and TREE as USFF, how is BOOK written?
explanation: Both examples move every letter one place forward, so BOOK becomes C, P, P, L: CPPL. The near miss CPPK leaves the last letter unmoved, which is the slip to watch for in four-letter codes.

text: If WATER is written as YCVGT, how is FIRE written in the same code?
explanation: Each letter moves two places forward: W-Y, A-C, T-V, E-G, R-T. So F-H, I-K, R-T, E-G, giving HKTG. One place forward gives GJSF and one back gives EHQD.

text: In a code, 'pit na lo' means 'bring hot water', 'na ro mi' means 'water is cold' and 'lo mi da' means 'bring the cold'. Which word means 'water'?
explanation: 'na' is in the first and second phrases, and the only English word those two share is 'water'. Cross-checking: 'lo' is in the first and third, which share 'bring'; 'mi' is in the second and third, which share 'cold'.

text: If in a code A=1, B=2 and so on, and the code for a word is the SUM of its letters, what is the code for CAB?
explanation: C is 3, A is 1 and B is 2, so the sum is 6. Reading the letters as a three-digit number (312) or forgetting one of them are the two ways this goes wrong.

text: If MONDAY is written as NPOEBZ, which day is written as GSJEBZ?
explanation: The code moves each letter one place forward, so decoding moves one back: G-F, S-R, J-I, E-D, B-A, Z-Y, giving FRIDAY. Six letters rules out SUNDAY and SATURDAY by length alone.

text: In a code GARDEN is written as 743259, each letter standing for one digit. How is DANGER written in the same code?
explanation: Read the mapping off GARDEN letter by letter: G=7, A=4, R=3, D=2, E=5, N=9. DANGER is D, A, N, G, E, R, which is 2, 4, 9, 7, 5, 3 = 249753. The distractors are the same six digits in the order of other anagrams, so the only way through is to build the mapping first and then spell the new word.

text: What is the area of a rectangle? I. Its length is 12 cm. II. Its perimeter is 36 cm.
options: Statement I alone is sufficient|Statement II alone is sufficient|Either statement alone is sufficient|Both together are needed, and both together are sufficient|Even both together are not sufficient
explanation: I alone gives no breadth. II alone allows many rectangles with perimeter 36. Together, length 12 and perimeter 36 give a breadth of 6 and an area of 72 square centimetres. Both together are needed, and both together are sufficient.

text: How old is Meera? I. She is 5 years older than her brother. II. Her brother will be 20 next year.
options: Statement I alone is sufficient|Statement II alone is sufficient|Either statement alone is sufficient|Both together are needed, and both together are sufficient|Even both together are not sufficient
explanation: I alone has no anchor and II alone says nothing about Meera. Together, the brother is 19 now, so Meera is 24. Both together are needed, and both together are sufficient.

text: Is the integer n even? I. n squared is even. II. n is divisible by 6.
options: Statement I alone is sufficient|Statement II alone is sufficient|Either statement alone is sufficient|Both together are needed, and both together are sufficient|Even both together are not sufficient
explanation: I is enough on its own: if n squared is even then n is even, because the square of an odd number is odd. II is also enough, since every multiple of 6 is a multiple of 2. Either statement alone is sufficient.

text: What was the mean mark of a class? I. The class has 40 students. II. The marks ranged from 32 to 96.
options: Statement I alone is sufficient|Statement II alone is sufficient|Either statement alone is sufficient|Both together are needed, and both together are sufficient|Even both together are not sufficient
explanation: A count and a range say nothing about the total, and the mean needs the total. Any mean between 32 and 96 is consistent with both. Even both together are not sufficient — which is a real answer and not a trick.

text: What is the cost price of an article? I. It was sold for Rs 1,200 at a profit of 20%. II. The profit was Rs 200.
options: Statement I alone is sufficient|Statement II alone is sufficient|Either statement alone is sufficient|Both together are needed, and both together are sufficient|Even both together are not sufficient
explanation: I gives the cost on its own: a selling price of 1,200 at 20% profit means 1,200 x 100/120 = 1,000. II gives a profit with no selling price, so the cost could be anything. Statement I alone is sufficient. (The two happen to agree, since a cost of 1,000 does yield a profit of 200 -- agreement is what a well-set pair looks like, not a reason to need both.)

text: In which year did a student join the college? I. She completed a four-year course in 2025. II. She joined two years after her sister, who joined in 2019.
options: Statement I alone is sufficient|Statement II alone is sufficient|Either statement alone is sufficient|Both together are needed, and both together are sufficient|Even both together are not sufficient
explanation: I gives 2021 by subtraction. II gives 2021 directly. Either statement alone is sufficient, and the two agreeing is a sign the question is well set rather than a reason to need both.

text: Is a quadrilateral a square? I. All four sides are equal. II. All four angles are equal.
options: Statement I alone is sufficient|Statement II alone is sufficient|Either statement alone is sufficient|Both together are needed, and both together are sufficient|Even both together are not sufficient
explanation: I alone admits a rhombus and II alone admits a rectangle. Together, equal sides and equal angles make a square. Both together are needed, and both together are sufficient — this is the cleanest example of two conditions that are each necessary and neither sufficient.

text: How many students passed a test? I. 80% of those who sat it passed. II. 150 students sat it.
options: Statement I alone is sufficient|Statement II alone is sufficient|Either statement alone is sufficient|Both together are needed, and both together are sufficient|Even both together are not sufficient
explanation: A percentage with no base and a base with no percentage are each useless. Together, 80% of 150 is 120. Both together are needed, and both together are sufficient.
